#1342. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

The pace of the game was slow and Villarreal were in control until the later stages of the half. Koumas and Cody Gakpo created a chance and from the corner that resulted Mac Allister headed in Tsimikas’s cross. Liverpool were up and running. Ngumoha’s cross from the left was unwisely left by Cardona for Araújo to score and the game was level.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

Then came Ngumoha’s big second half, creating the third for Mac Allister. The teenager went past Cardona and the substitute Juan Foyth in a couple of strides. Wirtz dispatched the fourth from Gakpo’s ball.

Even so there was still time for Liverpool to show that they had sacrificed some defensive stability. The absence of a right-back cost them when substitute Tani Oluwaseyi ran into that area of the pitch to score Villarreal’s third late on. The third win of Liverpool’s Champions League season puts them second in the 36-team super-table, and behind defending champions Paris St-Germain only on goal difference.

Liverpool are also seeing a new star emerge. Ngumoha might be the most expensive academy signing in the game’s modern history but alongside the £100m men he looks like a risk that was worth taking.

We have said all night about momentum, and talking about how they Liverpool will play against Brighton at the weekend, I’ll be amazed if Rio [Ngumoha] doesn’t start because of the momentum that he has got from this game.

You see the fans, you see how everyone got a lift by him and that’s what they need at the weekend, they need someone to lift them.

They are flying. Their confidence is through the roof. A similar style to Villarreal. They are second in everything after Barcelona. It has been a good game to prepare and we will use it.

I am really happy with Rio. He is trying to improve everything and we are trying to correct things. He played a lot on the left and know he is playing a lot on the right and he has adapted really well. We encourage him always. Even defensively as well he is improving. He has become a more complete player – and we must not forget he is 18!

Rio Ngumoha was magnificent tonight. Such a threat, and he dedicated himself to his tasks. On the ball this kid has so much potential, and I say kid, but he’s a young man. He has so much quality and it’s stuff that you can’t teach to be honest.

What he does with the ball at his feet, that is God given ability, and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he said in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that about him.

I’m not tall but I love going in the box. I really like it. They know I like to attack the near post. I scored in the World Cup as well. It was a good header. The second goal, Rio, was amazing. I talk with him about cutting it back on the floor.

It’s not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it’s something I got from him.

Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn’t right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don’t like to compare. I’m feeling good.

A lot of things happened today. They were much better than us in the first half and we were much better in the second half. When we’ve been under pressure, we answered well. When we relaxed, we made mistakes. You cannot relax against very good opposition. I value the win.

We have to know that if we don’t go to the limit, it will be difficult. We are facing very good teams. It’s good to come back but we’ve started losing too many goals this season.

Nine points from a possible nine for Liverpool in the Champions League, but they made hard work of it. Some dysfunction was probably to be expected after Iraola decided to start without Mac Allister, Isak, Wirtz and Barcola, but their defensive structure was unzipped far too easily at times.

Pape Gueye floats a cross straight down the throat of Alisson. A wasted opportunity for Villarreal. But still a couple of minutes to play.

Florian Wirtz has been readied for action and will soon enter the fray. You would think these will be the kind of conditions in which he will excel. He needs to. Liverpool are lucky to be level.

Plenty for Andoni Iraola to be annoyed about, but as a spectacle this has been far more entertaining than initially assumed.

Better from Liverpool with Nyoni driving forward and the ball almost running into the path of Gravenberch for a strike from the edge of the box. Villarreal diligent in their defensive work though, no clear sight of goal for the Liverpool players so far.

Anyone who is experiencing Anfield on a European night for the first time will be wondering what all the fuss is about. The flag was eventually raised for offside, but Villarreal were in behind the Liverpool defence again after a misplaced Van Dijk pass. Liverpool have not got themselves out of the blocks at all. They have lost possession too cheaply and look vulnerable defensively.

Buchanan with a teasing low cross through the Liverpool penalty area, and the winger is justified when looking quizzically at his team-mates. If one of the yellow shirts had gambled they would have had a tap in.

Villarreal then throw a punch of their own down the other end, with Saliba turning and shooting at the edge of the box. Deflected, and Villarreal have a corner. Delivery is poor and Liverpool clear.

The Spanish team are moving the ball around with assurance, some nice touches from Saliba in their midfield (the Canada international is no relation to the Arsenal centre-back).

Hats off to Villarreal coach Inigo Perez, who is not wearing a hat or, indeed, a coat. Polo shirt and slacks for the young Spanish coach.

Quick feet in the box to beat his man and fashion a yard for a strike, but his shot is blocked. Ngumoha is playing on Liverpool’s right tonight with Gakpo on the opposite flank.

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

Manchester United’s new manager Mauricio Pochettino is keen to strengthen up front this January and has four main names on his wish-list, as first revealed in a Daily Briefing exclusive earlier today.

Sources in the agents industry have informed me that the Red Devils are ready to spend big when it comes to backing Pochettino this January, but they are also assessing a wide range of targets.

One of the more exciting names being mentioned is one of Europe’s most in-form centre-forwards, with a stunning record of 19 goals in 19 games in all competitions so far this season.

The player in question is Benfica front-man Vangelis Pavlidis. I’ve reported here recently on Tottenham and Barcelona also being keen on the prolific Greece international, but we can now add United to that list.

“Pochettino is eager to make sure United have more of a goal threat,” one source said, speaking anonymously to protect relationships. “He’s already been discussing names, and Vangelis Pavlidis is someone who fits the bill.”

This has been backed up by others, while I’m also reliably told that Galatasaray striker Victor Osimhen is someone Pochettino would be really keen to work with. For now, this is considered less realistic due to the player’s high transfer fee and wage demands, but Pochettino was also a key driving force pushing to sign him for Chelsea, with a deal getting quite advanced before ultimately falling through.

Pavlidis could be more realistic and is understood to be open to a move to the Premier League. The 27-year-old ticks all the boxes as an immediate upgrade on the injury-prone Benjamin Sesko, while his age doesn’t necessarily pose too much of a threat to the young Slovenia international’s long-term development once he’s back to full fitness.

As previously reported, former Brentford striker Ivan Toney is also someone United have on their list. Though this predates Pochettino’s arrival, the England international is someone well known to the 54-year-old and his openness to coming back to the Premier League could make him a good short-term option if they cannot land their more ambitious targets.

Finally, multiple sources have also told me that Borussia Dortmund striker Serhou Guirassy is likely to be one to watch. The 30-year-old is not at the top of the club’s list, but he’s been monitored for some time and is seen as someone who could do a job as a rotation option.

Pochettino is also likely to be given new defenders to work with in January, though I’m less clear on the priorities for that department for now.

Jacobo Ramon is a long-term target but unlikely to be available in the middle of the season. There has been a hint of a link with Villarreal and USA full-back Alex Freeman, but nothing too concrete at this stage.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

It’s certainly clear that MUFC could do with a new signing or two at both centre-back and left-back, so it remains to be seen which of those will be prioritised.

I’ll be back with updates when I have them, but for now the main thing I’m hearing is the striker links which have the potential to be quite exciting.

#1340. Openda doubt as Juventus ready to reconsider Lyon loan

Juventus could have a low-cost boost for their attack in January by bringing Lois Openda back early from his Olympique Lyonnais loan or finding him a different club.

The Bianconeri are struggling to get goals, not helped by the injury crisis ruling out Kenan Yildiz, Francisco Conceicao, Nico Gonzalez and Arkadiusz Milik for weeks or even months at a time.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, there is an intriguing solution to bolster the options for coach Luciano Spalletti without spending any money.

The idea is to interrupt Openda’s loan experience at Olympique Lyonnais after just six months and bring him back to Turin during the January transfer window.

The 26-year-old was sent out on loan for €3.5m, and has made 10 competitive appearances for the French side, scoring two goals with one assist.

However, his last game was on October 9, when sustaining a fracture against RC Lens, and is expected back on the field next month.

In his absence, Lyon have parted company with coach Paulo Fonseca and brought in Carlos Vicens, whose idea of a striker is someone with very different characteristics to Openda.

If the Belgian is not getting regular playing time in Lyon, then it is likely he will either try to find another club to join on loan for the rest of the season, or even return to base and try his hand at Juve again.

He was considered a very expensive mistake from RB Leipzig for €46m between the loan and obligation to buy, managing only two goals in 34 games for the Bianconeri.

#1339. Record-breaking Ebola outbreak: phone data reconstruct first weeks of spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock

Epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared. The authors say the study findings reveal how surveillance systems failed to detect signals of the disease early on and enabled it to spread rapidly.

It is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was announced. The number of confirmed infections has risen to more than 10,000 and 5,198 people have died, making this the largest Bundibugyo outbreak so far. There are no licenced vaccines or approved treatments specifically for Bundibugyo, which has complicated efforts to control it.

The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May after laboratory tests confirmed the first case, a person from Ituri province in the country’s northeast, was infected with the Bundibugyo strain. Around the same time, suspected cases were being reported in several DRC locations, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia and Nyankunde in Ituri, and Butembo, Katwa and Goma in the neighbouring province of North Kivu. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May, citing infections among health-care workers, the geographical spread of cases and clusters of undocumented deaths. Researchers strongly suspect that the virus had been spreading in the region months earlier.

To understand how the outbreak spread so quickly, the researchers looked at anonymized mobile-phone data to trace the movement of people between areas.

Although the first confirmed case was identified on 15 May, the study reports that the person had symptoms as early as 25 April.

The team found that people travelling out of Mongbwalu, Bunia and Rwampara between 24 April and 24 May helped to predict which health zones would report infections by 1 June. For instance, areas close to the initial centres were at greater risk of infections, the study found.

The risk of infections rose again in places 150–200 kilometres away from the initial outbreak centres because people travelled to larger towns and cities along established routes, says study co-author Pierre Akilimali, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) in Kinshasa.

The authors say the findings show that people movement was a key driver of the rapid spread in the early phases of the outbreak.

“These are very important findings which reinforce what we initially knew at the onset of the outbreak,” says Tambe Akem, an independent public-health consultant based in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03666-z

Ebengo. D. M. et al. Science https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aej4586 (2026).

#1337. Pedro Neto is sent off for two yellow cards in under two minutes before bizarre touchline clash with Craig Bellamy - as Portugal beat Wales with Bruno Fernandes on target

Published: 17:34 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:49 EST, 17 November 2026

Chelsea star Pedro Neto lost his cool while playing for Portugal in their win over Wales as he received two yellow cards in as many minutes before clashing with opposing manager Craig Bellamy.

The Blues winger had in fact scored in the game, netting his side's second goal at the Cardiff City Stadium, but saw his game fall apart in the second-half.

He was first booked for a high challenge on the back of Brennan Johnson's leg – a tackle which some may argue could have been a red in itself.

One minute and 59 seconds later, he was shown his second yellow when he slid in on Johnson again. He didn't appear to make too much contact, if any, but left the Wales man sprawling to avoid it.

German referee Sven Jablonski showed no hesitation in sending Neto off, but the winger wasn't going to take it lying down.

He had to be held back by captain Bruno Fernandes as he tried to confront Johnson, and seemingly managed to shout in his direction before reluctantly making his way off the field.

Pedro Neto was sent off while playing for Portugal against Wales after two yellow cards in under two minutes

He also had a confrontation with Wales manager Craig Bellamy (right) as he left the field of play

Before that, though, he had a conversation with Wales boss Craig Bellamy, with officials initially trying to separate the two, with Neto looking angry.

Bellamy, though, spoke to Neto and embraced him before finally walking down the tunnel.

The 26-year-old will now serve a one-game suspension, meaning he will miss the first leg of Portugal's Nations League quarter-final, which will be played in March.

Jorge Jesus's side secured top spot in their group with the win over Wales, which was achieved by Carlos Forbs's 70th-minute goal.

Fernandes had opened the scoring for his side in the 11th minute, but David Brooks and Sorba Thomas gave Wales an unlikely lead.

That was until Neto levelled things up just before half-time, and Forbs scored the winner, with ten-man Portugal able to hold on for all three points.

Wales finished bottom of the group with one win – against Norway – and five defeats from their six matches.

Captain Ben Davies said after the game: 'We showed a lot of character and we've shown good effort in these games where we've just come up short from a results perspective.

After expressing his frustration, the Chelsea star had to be directed off the field by captain Bruno Fernandes (right)

He had in fact scored for his side in the game, bringing them level before the half-time interval

'There is a lot to take from this going into the games in March and we have to feel confident because we've been playing well.

'We know the boys up top can be so dangerous, and if teams want to come here and play man-for-man against us, we've got a lot of speed and we have to be good on the ball. That comes with risk sometimes, like you saw with the chances that they had, but I'd rather play this way and go toe-to-toe with these teams and have a go.

'We competed in the campaign and we were not a million miles off like the table might suggest. I thought we put in some very good performances, we just wished we had some better results.'

Neto, meanwhile, will now return to his club side Chelsea ahead of a busy Christmas period.

He has started all but one Premier League game so far and has been a key player under new manager Xabi Alonso.

The Blues will take on Leeds at Stamford Bridge this weekend as club football returns.

#1334. Gary Neville is Wrong: Man Utd Must Sell Harry Maguire Before Matthijs De Ligt

Manchester United are set to embark on a new era at Old Trafford under Mauricio Pochettino, after the Argentine officially became manager on Wednesday.

The 54-year-old replaces Michael Carrick in the dugout and leaves his role as USMNT manager on the back of an 8-0 aggregate win over Haiti in the Nations League, helping them qualify for the semi-finals.

His first game in charge of Man Utd will see him travel to Anfield to take on arch rivals Liverpool, but regardless of what happens in that game on Sunday, there are plenty of things that he must sort out before he can really revolutionise Man Utd and get the squad in the right shape.

The most important thing will be who is part of his squad. A number of players have been linked with moves away from the club, while it's inevitable that Pochettino will also want to bring in his own players to help him implement his style and system as quickly as possible.

A defensive rebuild is reportedly planned for the 2027 summer transfer window, with a number of players out of contract and others on the chopping block for a potential sale, as INEOS look to raise funds to be able to upgrade a defence which has conceded the most goals of any team in Europe's top five leagues.

Diogo Dalot has been heavily criticised in recent times, but surprisingly, club legend Gary Neville has come out in his defence in a recent podcast appearance on Stick to United, and claimed that a number of other players should be sold before him.

"Dalot isn't Denis Irwin, lets be really clear. They shouldn't even be mentioned in the same breath. But I'd be getting rid of a few before Dalot," he said.

"Dalot got booed at Old Trafford last week, and I was really surprised by that. I think he's such an easy target, and I know that's going to be unpopular. I look at full-backs really closely... I'd be getting Mazraoui well gone before him. I'd be getting [Lisandro] Martinez gone well before him. I'd be getting De Ligt gone well before him."

Mark Goldbridge then stepped in and stated that he disagreed with the comments on De Ligt, but Neville doubled down.

"He's got one big problem; he doesn't play football.

"If a player is injury-prone and doesn't play football, just because he hasn't played doesn't mean to say that he should go above a player who's playing every week and throwing his hand up.

"You want someone who is reliable and can play.

Neville's comments about De Ligt are surprising, especially considering the fact the Netherlands star is only just returning after a serious back injury which left him sidelined for almost an entire year.

Prior to that, De Ligt was establishing himself as a regular in the team. He played in all 13 Premier League games last season before picking up his injury against Crystal Palace, while he made 29 appearances in the Premier League in his debut campaign before that.

That shows that he is generally reliable and available, and one long-term injury shouldn't be enough for the team to give up on him. But more pertinent is the fact he's easily one of the better defenders at the club.

Physically, he has a similar profile to the much-maligned Harry Maguire, but he is more mobile and much better on the ball, while also being able to duel in battles with defenders and be dominant in the air. Add to the fact that he is still only 27, too, and it's clear that Maguire should be shown the exit door way before the former Ajax and Bayern Munich star.

Maguire is out of contract at the end of the season and his performances have already begun to dwindle. His form this season has been poor, and his lack of athleticism remains a huge issue. He's also on big wages, which would be easy to get off the books by letting his contract run down.

Neville is known to be a big fan of an English core, and it seems that he is letting that cloud his judgement. De Ligt is far superior to Maguire in every way as a footballer and defender, and if either of them are to leave in the summer, then it's a no-brainer.

#1330. Under-17 World Cup Graduates Who Won A Senior World Cup

The FIFA U-17 World Cup has long been a shop window for football's next generation, but going from teenage promise to a senior world champion is another matter entirely.

Since the first edition in 1985, just 25 players have been named in a U-17 World Cup squad and gone on to lift the real thing. Some starred as teenagers, others barely registered, and a handful suffered heartbreak at youth level before finding redemption on the biggest stage.

Here is every U-17 World Cup graduate to become a world champion.

Alessandro Del Piero (1991), Gianluigi Buffon (1993), Francesco Totti (1993)

Iker Casillas, Xavi (1997), Pepe Reina (1999), Andrés Iniesta, Fernando Torres (2001), Cesc Fàbregas, David Silva (2003)

Roman Weidenfeller (1997), Toni Kroos (2007), Mario Götze, Shkodran Mustafi (2009)

Emiliano Martínez, Nicolás Tagliafico (2009), Exequiel Palacios (2015)

Aymeric Laporte (2011, for France), Ferran Torres, Eric García (2017), Pedri (2019), Pau Cubarsí (2023)

Emmanuel Petit was the first U-17 graduate to become a world champion. He represented France in Canada in 1987, when the competition was still an under-16 tournament, and Les Bleus finished second in a group containing Brazil, Australia and Saudi Arabia before bowing out in the quarter-finals.

Eleven years later, the Arsenal midfielder was integral to Aimé Jacquet's side on home soil. His first international goal was the winner in a 2-1 group-stage victory over Denmark, and he saved the best until last in the final, supplying the corner for Zinedine Zidane's opener before sealing a 3-0 win over Brazil in stoppage time.

Ronaldinho, one of the greatest dribblers in football history, remains the only man to win both tournaments. Brazil swept through their group in Egypt in 1997, and the teenage playmaker converted a late penalty in a 4-0 semi-final rout of Germany before the Seleção beat Ghana in the final.

Five years on, he completed the 'Three Rs' alongside Ronaldo and Rivaldo. He scored from the spot against China, but his defining moment came in the quarter-final against England, a looping 50th-minute free-kick over David Seaman that settled a 2-1 win. He was sent off seven minutes later and missed the semi-final, but returned as Brazil beat Germany in the final.

Italy's 2006 triumph was built on two forgettable youth campaigns. Alessandro Del Piero was part of the host nation's squad in 1991 and scored in a 2-2 draw with China, but Italy failed to escape their group.

Two years later in Japan, a 15-year-old Buffon and Totti fared even worse, finishing bottom of their group with Totti scoring Italy's only goal of the tournament, against Mexico.

All three delivered in Germany. Gianluigi Buffon, one of the best goalkeepers of all time, conceded just twice in seven matches, Francesco Totti fired a 95th-minute penalty to knock out Australia in the last 16, and Del Piero sealed the extra-time semi-final win over the hosts before converting Italy's fourth spot-kick in the final shootout against France.

No nation has drawn more from the tournament than Spain. Iker Casillas and Xavi helped La Rojita finish third in 1997, Jose Reina kept goal in 1999, and Iniesta and Fernando Torres were in the side that exited at the group stage in 2001.

Then came the nearly men of 2003. Cesc Fàbregas won the Golden Ball and finished joint top scorer with five goals, playing alongside David Silva, but Spain lost the final 1-0 to Brazil.

Redemption arrived in Johannesburg as Spain's young talents grew into world-beaters, as they dominated international for years, putting together one of the longest unbeaten runs in international football and winning Euro 2008 and 2012, with the World Cup sandwiched in between those two triumphs. Casillas claimed the Golden Glove after twice denying Arjen Robben in the final, and in the 116th minute substitute Fàbregas teed up Iniesta, one of the greatest midfielders in football history, for the winner.

Toni Kroos announced himself in South Korea in 2007, captaining Germany to third place and collecting the Golden Ball after scoring five goals. Mario Götze and Shkodran Mustafi followed in Nigeria two years later, where Germany fell to eventual champions Switzerland in the knockout rounds, while Roman Weidenfeller had been part of the side that finished fourth back in 1997.

In Brazil, Kroos was imperious, scoring twice in the 7-1 semi-final demolition of the hosts and Götze came off the bench to volley the 113th-minute winner in the final. Mustafi's tournament ended when he tore a thigh muscle against Algeria in the last 16, and Weidenfeller went unused as Manuel Neuer's back-up.

Benjamin Mendy made three appearances at the 2011 tournament in Mexico, where a France squad also containing future Spain centre-back Aymeric Laporte reached the quarter-finals.

Seven years later, he was lucky to make the plane at all. Having ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament early in his first season at Manchester City, he only returned to action in the spring before the tournament.

His contribution in Russia was modest. After sitting out the opening two group games, the left-back came on in the 50th minute of a goalless draw with Denmark, and those 40 minutes were his only action as France went on to win the tournament.

Emiliano Martínez and Nicolás Tagliafico were in the Argentina squad that met Götze and Mustafi's Germany in the group stage in Nigeria in 2009. Götze put the Germans ahead inside eight minutes, but Argentina hit back in the second half to win 2-1, an early meeting between two groups of future world champions. Exequiel Palacios had a tougher introduction in 2015, as Argentina finished bottom of their group after a 4-0 defeat to Germany.

In Qatar, Martínez became a national hero. One of the best goalkeepers in the world, he won the Golden Glove and, after a 3-3 draw with France, saved from Kingsley Coman in the shootout before Aurélien Tchouaméni sent his kick wide.

Ferran Torres and Eric García knew youth heartbreak. Torres scored twice in India in 2017, including in the semi-final win over Mali, before Spain surrendered a two-goal lead to lose the final 5-2 to England. Pedri's Spain were thrashed 6-1 by France in 2019, and Cubarsí's side fell 1-0 to eventual winners Germany in the 2023 quarter-finals. Laporte, meanwhile, had played for France in 2011.

In New Jersey, all five featured. Cubarsí and Laporte started, Pedri came on in the 62nd minute, García replaced Laporte in extra time, and substitute Torres struck in the 106th minute to beat Argentina and give Spain a second star.

Spain's 2026 World Cup hero explains why he wore the MAGA-style hat following praise from US President Donald Trump

Not every U-17 graduate got a fairytale ending. Argentina's 2014 final starting line-up included four of them, and all four lost 1-0 to Germany.

Martínez is the latest addition. Already a world champion, he made a reported 11 saves in the 2026 final, but it was not enough to stop Ferran Torres.

#1329. 'We felt like medieval peasants coming up against a king': Insiders relive the battle to rid Blackpool of the Oystons, from tangerines stuffed in knickers to a bright orange GTI - and why 'insider dealing' claims mean club isn't out of the woods yet

Published: 07:55 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EST, 17 November 2026

In the south London pub where they are readying themselves for a League One match with AFC Wimbledon, Blackpool fans who fought for their club’s heart and soul, 10 years ago, receive a message informing them that half the squad have gone down with a sickness bug so severe that the starting XI will be very unusual.

Three players are too ill to leave the team hotel, the goalkeeper selected is yet to feature in the league this season and the EFL don’t consider this predicament serious enough to cancel the game. The club are already on a run of five defeats in seven.

Moments like this reveal the Blackpool fanbase’s deep sense of perspective, born of their long and often wretched fight to kick out one of British football’s most detested owners, Owen Oyston.

‘We’re still here and we’re watching our club home and away,’ says Andy Higgins, chair of the Blackpool Supporters Trust. ‘We have a good relationship with the club,’ says his friend Dave Ragozzino, with Higgins in the Earlsfield pub. ‘The club are asking us to tell fans what’s going on, and they know we will help. Ten years ago, our club’s owners were suing us.’

The story of the campaign which brought these fans and many more together is told in a superb new documentary The Battle for Blackpool, which screens this week, capturing its spirit, imagination and intelligence.

Oyston and his son Karl have both cooperated with the documentary-makers. Oyston Snr, wearing dark shades and his trademark fedora, is interviewed at his stately home in the Forest of Bowland, while his son Karl, clearly still consumed with hate and contempt for fans, is filmed clay pigeon shooting across their estate.

Blackpool fans watch their team fall to another League One defeat, at AFC Wimbledon on Saturday

The Tangerines are just two points above the relegation zone having lost five out of their last seven league fixtures

Their supporters fought a long and wretched battle against the club's former owner Owen Oyston (pictured in 2017)

The film’s stars are the supporters who led the fight – Christine Seddon, Tim Fielding, Ragozzino, two fans in a Mk1 tangerine Golf GTI and twin sisters of advancing years who embraced the campaign’s guerilla tactics.

Oyston Jr, who chaired the club at his mother’s request after his father was jailed for rape in 1996, tells the documentary-makers: ‘My father likes football. I didn’t.’

It was after he’d stumbled on a managerial genius in Ian Holloway, who took the club into the Premier League for a season in 2010-11, that a full sense of the family’s greed and entitlement became clear.

The Mail on Sunday's Nick Harris revealed that Oyston Snr had paid himself £11million out of the Premier League jackpot, while critics say virtually all the club appeared to get out of promotion was a new sprinkler system. The fight against the Oystons took hold. The Blackpool Supporters Trust, then chaired by Fielding, was its strategic and political wing, flanked by the imaginative sabotage activities of the Tangerine Knights group.

A plot to smuggle tennis balls into the ground for a home match against Burnley, in April 2014, and collectively throw them on the pitch, provides one of the documentary’s many glorious sections. Fans stuffed the missiles into their pants, socks and bras.

‘I had them in my knickers,’ says Christine Atkinson, who is interviewed with her twin sister, Pauline O’Rourke. ‘I didn’t have tennis balls. I had tangerines. It was softer. Less uncomfortable!’

The family of Karl Oyston mocked the tennis ball protest on social media. But it was when his father began suing ordinary fans, some pensioners, for criticising him that the protest escalated.

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr tells the film-makers.

‘I had tangerines in my knickers,’ says Pauline O'Rourke (right), who is interviewed with her twin sister, Christine Atkinson, in the documentary about Blackpool's fight to get rid of the owners

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr (pictured in 2010) tells the film-makers

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke, interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Koudellas inside the tangerine GTI, parked up on Blackpool’s South Shore – one of the film’s many wonderful touches.

Ragozzino lost his job and faced a £150,000 legal suit. Fielding, a solicitor, was told it would cost more than £250,000 to defend himself against Oyston’s legal action. The Oystons forced him to pay them £10,000 in cash and issue a public apology.

Karl Oyston reveals how much he revelled in the war with fans, delighting in the ‘Oyston Out’ personalised number plate his wife bought for Christmas to maintain the mockery. ‘She thought it was highly amusing. Which it was,’ he relates.

Suing elderly Blackpool fans was his father’s idea, he says. ‘But as soon as the board makes a decision, you fight to the death to support it.’

Oyston Snr maintains he was perfectly entitled to pay himself £11m of the Premier League money. ‘Why wouldn’t we? Why shouldn’t we?’ he asks. ‘We own the company. We’d had 25 years of pouring money down the drain without the least prospect of seeing any of it ever again.’

It was Fielding who came up with the game-changing strategy – persuading minority shareholder Valeri Belokon to mount a successful legal challenge against the Oystons, eventually clearing the way for Simon Sadler, a Hong Kong-based financier and Blackpudlian to buy the club.

It’s not been a bed of roses these past few years. An interim club board, formed after Oyston was ousted, included Ben Hatton, later chief operating officer at Aston Villa, former Inter Milan CEO Mike Bolingbroke and Fielding. But a succession of good leaders have left.

Brett Gerrity, a one-time close friend of Sadler who persuaded him to buy the club, resigned in 2023. The two no longer get on. Ben Mansford, respected ex-CEO at Leeds and Barnsley, also unexpectedly left. Former sporting director David Downes was recently made CEO. Amid these comings and goings, Sadler has not appointed a successful manager since Neil Critchley left to assist Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa in 2022.

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke (right), interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Coudellas inside the tangerine GTI

Christine Seddon was a leading figure in the fight to rid Blackpool of the Oystons

None of this has affected fans’ views of Sadler, a boyhood Blackpool fan whose investment is still giving the club a top eight budget in League One. He has spent money on upgrades to the stadium and training ground and the team’s playing surface is excellent.

But his own future at Bloomfield Road is in doubt. He is on trial in Hong Kong over accusations of insider dealing linked to his former hedge fund and could face a prison sentence if convicted.

That would mean him failing the EFL Owners’ and Directors’ Test and he would seemingly have to sell. The verdict in that case is expected next February. Sadler, who has pleaded not guilty to the charges, has revealed little of any contingencies he might have made. He is thought to be prepared to sell the club, though only if the buyer will be a true custodian.

‘He’s acutely aware of not putting Blackpool right back where it was with Oyston,’ says one source.

‘The club is so much better and professional than it used to be,' Seddon tells us. ‘But we are short of football business experience. We don’t have a proper board at the moment.

'Hedge fund management – our owner’s world – does not always translate well into football. It’s a steep learning curve.’

Oyston Snr revealed in a recent interview that he wants to buy the club back and gift a majority share to fans. ‘In 2015, we suggested to him that he walk away and leave the club’s assets to the fans,’ says Seddon.

‘He ignored us, yet now he’s suggesting this. These are deluded ramblings. Simon Sadler would not give Oyston the time of day.’

'When I hear some fans complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?”'

Karl Oyston tells the documentary-makers that he has not spoken to his 92-year-old father since the family’s 32-year ownership of the club ended in 2019. Will he ever see him again, he is asked. ‘No. That ship’s sailed,’ he replies.

Blackpool, backed by a loud, strong away following, fell to a 1-0 defeat at Wimbledon and boss Ian Evatt’s job will be on the line when they face fellow-strugglers Wigan on Saturday, so the film is a particularly timely reminder of how far this club’s fans have come.

‘Yes, we want results to be better,’ Seddon says. ‘But when I hear some complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?” Our club became an opportunity for people who were dismantling it for their own benefit. There were times when we thought we would lose it altogether.

'But we’re now in a place where we were beginning to believe we would never be. We’re thankful for that.’

The Battle for Blackpool will premiere in the UK on November 21 on Sky Documentaries and streaming service NOW

#1328. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

The detail on United’s passes has been so poor thus far, with Como picking up loose balls all over the pitch.

Penalty shout for Como! Da Cunha, Douvikas and Baturina combine expertly through the middle, trading the ball with cultured one-touch passes. Baturina is felled by Maguire inside United’s box just as he was gearing up to shoot, but neither the referee nor the VAR are minded to intervene. There is a touch, but it does seem very slight.

United have gone with the box midfield once more, with Fernandes rolling inside as a false 9. Como are counteracting United’s movements through Paz dropping in, so Carrick’s men are struggling to take control of the central zones.

Mbeumo bursts towards the by-line but Ramon gets back sharply to divert the ball behind for a corner, which is easily dealt with.

United drop into a deep block, forcing Como to build around the outside. The ball is worked to the adventurous Couto who loses his boot after an overzealous challenge from Cunha and he earns a free-kick for his troubles, but Da Cunha’s delivery fails to beat the first man.

Chance! Da Cunha plays a lovely through-ball into the right channel for Paz to gallop on to and he flashes the ball across the face of goal, but Maguire gets there before Douvikas and the ball is cleared.

United are struggling to string passes together as Paz cuts out a Lammens pass out from the back, but he cannot keep the ball in play.

United need to settle, and here they decide it best to keep hold of the ball for a while. There are a few sideways passes but the ball goes back to Como.

Valle makes a burst down the left and Dalot’s contact results in a foul, but the free-kick is not up to much.

Como 1 Manchester United 0 (Paz) Well, we said he was special! Como work the ball out to the right, with Da Cunha picking out Paz on the edge of the box. Neither of United’s centre-halves are minded to close the Argentine down, and he opens up his body before shaping the ball around Lammens and inside the far post. Golazo.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

#1326. 15 Best Premier League Centre-Backs Right Now (2026/27)

The art of defending, often overshadowed by the glitter of goals and assists, remains the backbone of every successful football side. No team has been able to dominate their respective league, or even individual competitions, without having a world-class back-line. Over the years, the Premier League has been home to some of the best centre-backs in world football. The likes of Rio Ferdinand, Tony Adams, John Terry, Vincent Kompany, and many, many, more spring to mind when thinking about whom the best of the best were.

The aforementioned quartet were arguably complete defenders, imperious in the air when required, solid in one-vs-one situations, and intelligent enough to position themselves in the right place to snuff out any danger. Today, modern-day centre-backs plying their trade in the English top-flight are meant to do all that and more, given the frantic pace of the league.

However, the current crop of defenders are truly some of the finest we've ever seen. Be it Liverpool's Virgil van Dijk, often labelled the best defender in recent memory, or Arsenal's William Saliba, crucial to Mikel Arteta's successful Premier League campaign during the 2025/26 season.

But who is the best of the best today? We've attempted to rank the best centre-backs in the league right now. We've considered each player's form from last season and the early weeks of the 2026/27 campaign, but have also factored in how good they have been historically too.

A Premier League institution for a decade, Everton's backline leader has been a consistent, old-school presence in the top flight for both the Toffees and Burnley. He has built on an impressive 2025/26 campaign, helping Everton to exceed expectations in the early weeks of the season. Tarkowski has contributed to Everton having one of the most formidable defences in the league, with the club well in the fight for European qualification. For David Moyes' side, he is indispensable.

The £52 million man has already established himself in Xabi Alonso's Chelsea side. The France international is one of the quickest centre-backs in the league, helping him to recover well and come out on top in 1v1 situations.

Lacroix earned his move to Stamford Bridge following an integral role in the highly successful Crystal Palace squad of recent seasons. With Palace, he won the UEFA Conference League, FA Cup, and the Community Shield, earning him his first France call-up and a spot in the World Cup squad.

Liverpool fans have been worrying about the post-Virgil van Dijk defence for some time now, but it seems that a successor has presented itself in Jeremy Jaquet. The 21-year-old was snapped up for £60 million after impressive displays for Rennes. The fee highlighted the centre-back's qualities. And in his debut season, the Frenchman has shown maturity beyond his years.

Jaquet hasn't looked out of place alongside his veteran Dutch partner, which speaks volumes of his potential. Now a senior France international, regularly partnering Ibrahima Konate, the player he has replaced, Jaquet looks more and more impressive with every game in the Premier League.

Andoni Iraola has quietly filled the hole left by Ibrahima Konate in Liverpool's defence.

Most bookies had Brentford down as one of the favourites to be relegated last season following Bryan Mbeumo and Yoane Wissa's departures and Thomas Frank ending his historic reign at the Gtech. But many forgot that the Bees still possessed one of the Premier League's most reliable defenders in Nathan Collins, who has been a rock for new manager Keith Andrews.

There are many reasons the West London outfit remains one of the toughest teams to play against, and Collins is one of them. The Irish defender has stepped up for Andrews with inspired performances, using his tall frame to good effect. Reports linked Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur with Collins last year, and such interest will only grow with each passing display from the Irishman.

Luka Vuskovic has quickly emerged as one of the Premier League's most exciting young defenders. A product of Hajduk Split's academy, he joined Tottenham before sealing a club-record £46 million move to Brighton in the summer of 2026. The 19-year-old Croatian towers over the competition at 6'4", defending on the front foot, and, unsurprisingly, offering a goalscoring threat from set-pieces. Vuskovic has anchored Brighton's backline during the 2026/27 season, helping them to disrupt the hierarchy of the traditional top six.

The top-flight is full of superstars, but there can only be one winner for each club.

One of the most versatile defenders in the league, Ezri Konsa can now call himself both an England World Cup representative and an Arsenal player. The Englishman's calm demeanour at the centre of Unai Emery's defence earned him a major move to Arsenal over the 2026 summer, joining the champions for £55 million.

And despite having Gabriel Magalhaes and William Saliba to contend with, as well as the likes of Jurrien Timber and Ben White vying for places across the backline, Konsa has already bedded into Arteta's side.

Jan Paul van Hecke had been colossal at the back for the Seagulls in recent years, representing another example of Brighton's exemplary scouting system in action. The Dutch international is considered one of the best centre-backs in the league, and his former boss at Brighton, Roberto De Zerbi, clearly hadn't forgotten about the towering defender when planning his summer spending in 2026.

The pair were reunited for £52 million, with van Hecke's stylish and attractive play out from the back now providing a solid bedrock for transition out of defence into attack for De Zerbi's side. Alongside Micky van de Ven, Tottenham have built themselves a defensive wall reinforced with solid Dutch steel.

The short, stocky Brazil international is a cult hero for Forest and for good reason. The defender is just as happy driving forward with the ball as he is diving in front of it and crunching into tackles. A great reader of the game, Murillo is well known for his interceptions and spotting danger, leading the league in defensive clearances during the 2024/25 season.

Murillo played in all 38 of Forest's Premier League games last season, highlighting his quality and durability, as the side also enjoyed a run to the semi-finals of the Europa League. It's hard to imagine the Premier League side without Murillo amongst its ranks.

The 20 greatest centre-backs in Premier League history, including Rio Ferdinand and John Terry, have been ranked in order.

Albeit injured for a fair chunk of his debut season in 2023, Micky van de Ven was a revolutionary signing under then-Spurs manager Ange Postecoglou. van de Ven’s incredible concoction of pace, power and high defensive IQ leant itself to both defensive obstinance and free-flowing attack.

An astute passer, too, there are not many flaws in the former Wolfsburg man’s skillset. The fastest man in the Premier League since records began, Roberto De Zerbi is building the backbone of his side around van de Ven and his compatriot van Hecke. After a tough few years for Tottenham, their fortunes seem to be turning at last. van de Ven's athleticism has been a huge part of the club's recent revival.

Pep Guardiola loves an adaptable defender and that's exactly what Josko Gvardiol was purchased to provide when he arrived at the Etihad in 2023. He proved to be one of the league's best left-backs, with his muscular frame at odds with his ability to support the attack. Gvardiol has been working well as both a left-back and a centre-back in a defensive three, such is his versatility.

The 24-year-old is already well past a century of appearances and could become one of the Cityzens' all-time greats when it's all said and done. Reliable even when City's form has dipped in recent years, Gvardiol is contributing at both ends too. Currently, he has 14 goals in all competitions for the club.

#1324. Wayne Rooney Named Surprise English Club With Most ‘Horrible’ Fans

Jamie Carragher was left stunned when Wayne Rooney named the English club with the most 'horrible' set of supporters.

Rooney retired back in January 2021, calling time on an illustrious career which spanned three different decades and four different clubs. After breaking through at Everton, the striker signed for Manchester United at the age of 18 in July 2004.

Making 559 appearances across 13 seasons for the north-west club, Rooney won five Premier League titles, an FA Cup, three League Cups, a Champions League and a Europa League during his time at Old Trafford.

Rooney returned to Everton in the latter stages of his career, before enjoying late stints at D.C. United and Derby County. He retired as one of the best strikers to ever play the game, with a combination of his goalscoring record and his technical proficiency placing him into this pantheon of greats.

Having played at the top level for so long, Rooney would have entertained millions of fans in numerous different stadiums throughout his career.

Scoring 253 goals for United, he naturally established himself as the talisman of Sir Alex Ferguson's successful side of the late 2000s and early 2010s, and this label would've come with ample abuse from fans of the Red Devils' greatest rivals.

The supporters of Liverpool and Manchester City in particular wouldn't have been the biggest fans of the striker, and certainly would've made these feelings known to Rooney loud and clear throughout matches.

However, Rooney surprisingly cited a different club when asked which team he felt had the most annoying supporters, and he went as far as describing these fans as 'horrible'— a claim which left Carragher shocked.

"As a player going... [a club] that had horrible fans was Blackpool," Rooney said on an episode of the Overlap back in 2025.

"Honestly, we played Blackpool away a few times and, like, god, they were horrible."

Rooney's answer elicited a hysterical laugh from Carragher, who chimed in on the conversation to remind people that his Liverpool team lost twice to the Tangerines in the 2010/11 campaign: "We [Liverpool] got beat by them two times in the same season in the Roy Hodgson years."

To this day, that was Blackpool's only season in the Premier League. The Lancashire club won promotion to the English top flight under Ian Holloway in the 2009/10 campaign, before going straight back down in their solitary season in the big time.

It didn't seem the Liverpudlian liked many players throughout his career, but there's one that stood out as his arch nemesis in the mid-2000s.

Rooney played against the Seasiders twice that year, visiting the intimidating 16,000-seater Bloomfield Road Stadium in January 2011. Clearly, the hostility Rooney felt inside the quaint seaside venue got to him, as United found themselves 2-0 down at half-time.

The legendary England centre-forward was hooked on 66 minutes, before the Red Devils staged a dramatic late comeback to emerge with a 3-2 victory. They'd go on to win the Premier League title.

#1323. Who needs sex? Kelp reproduce asexually when no mate is nearby

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Giorgia Guglielmi is a freelance writer in Basel, Switzerland.

Both male and female kelp were shown to be capable of reproduction without fertilization.Credit: Madelein_Wolf/Getty

When potential mates are scarce, some types of seaweed can take reproduction into their own hands, so to speak, according to a study published on 12 November in PLoS Biology1.

“Our findings highlight that kelp are even more flexible in their reproduction than previously appreciated,” says Daniel Liesner, a marine biologist at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel in Germany.

The brown algae, which provide food and shelter for marine life, “are really weird, they do all kinds of stuff”, says Reina Veenhof, an ecologist at the Scottish Association for Marine Science in Oban, UK. What’s interesting about the study is that it helps to explain how changes in gene activity allow kelp to reproduce in different ways, she says.

Scientists know that kelp can reproduce asexually, with unfertilized eggs developing into offspring. This process was even documented for one male strain2 — the PLoS Biology study shows that this wasn’t a one-off.

The ability of male reproductive cells to develop without fertilization is striking, says Olivier De Clerck, a seaweed biologist at Ghent University in Belgium. This is because, unlike eggs, sperm cells are small and have few resources to support development.

The researchers focused on Laminaria pallida, a species found along the Atlantic coasts of South Africa and Namibia. In the wild, 523 individual kelp showed no clear evidence of asexual reproduction.

By contrast, both microscopic male and female L. pallida grown in separate laboratory dishes could produce offspring without fertilization. During asexual reproduction, the gene expression in males changed, making them more similar to females.

However, when they were lab-grown in the presence of a member of the opposite sex, kelp favoured sexual reproduction, suggesting they can detect nearby partners through chemical signals.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03665-0

Liesner, D. et al. PLoS Biol. 24, e3004065 (2026).

Article  Google Scholar

Liboureau, P., Pearson, G. A., Serrão, E. A., Kreiner, A. & Martins, N. Eur. J. Phycol. 59, 232–241 (2024).

#1322. UEFA Nations League Draw: Date, Time, Live Stream & Who England Can Get

After England ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run, which was the longest in international men's football history, with their 3-2 win, Thomas Tuchel's side secured the top spot in their UEFA Nations League group, and will soon find out who they'll face in the quarter-finals.

As the draw takes place, eight of Europe's biggest nations will be paired up for two-legged ties in March, with a place at June's finals at stake. Portugal, France and Spain have all won the trophy, but we could see a new champion crowned in 2027.

Here's when the draw takes place, who's in it and how to watch.

The draw for the quarter-finals of the Nations League will take place at the UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland on Friday 20th November at 12:00 local time, or 11:00 GMT.

As well as finding out the match-ups for the quarter-finals, viewers will also find out who will face who in the promotion and relegation playoffs between Leagues A/B and B/C.

The first leg will take place between 25th-27th March 2027, during the March international break, with the return fixture kicking-off just days later, between 28th and 30th March. The four winners will go through to the Nations League Finals. Semi-final pairings will be established by another draw, with the losers taking a spot in the third-placed playoff, and the winners booking themselves a place in the final.

As winners of their group, England earned themselves a seeded spot in the draw, alongside France, Germany and Portugal, with the latter having won the tournament twice, including the most recent edition in 2024/25 when they beat Spain on penalties.

The unseeded side of the pot is made up of nations who finished as runners-up of their respective groups, namely Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain and Norway, who will play in their first ever Nations League Finals.

Winning their group ensured that England achieved a seeded spot in the draw. This means that they cannot face one of the other nations who won their group. A seeded spot also means that England will play the second-leg of the quarter-finals at home, which could play a significant role should they need a result.

England also cannot be drawn against anyone from their own group, meaning that a rematch against Spain is out of the question until the semi-finals. This leaves England's potential quarter-final opponents as Belgium, the Netherlands or Norway.

Fans can still follow the draw in real-time by tuning in for free to UEFA TV, or by watching on UEFA's official YouTube channel.

UEFA's official broadcast partners will also cover the draw in one form or another, with ITV, BBC and Sky Sports being useful networks for those based in the UK. In the USA, UEFA Nations League is shown on FOX Sports, Fubo and ViX.
