#1321. How Mauricio Pochettino's culture shock tactics will resurrect Man United: From 'Murderball' training that leaves players throwing up to telling Harry Kane to slim down and why even the smell of the kit must be spot on

Published: 21:00 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 17 November 2026

When the entertaining but ultimately rather pointless Ralf Rangnick was tasked with holding the fort as manager at Manchester United five years ago, he was asked whether his much-admired style of football – the high-intensity gegenpress aped by disciples such as Jurgen Klopp – could work with a team that had Cristiano Ronaldo, 36, and Edinson Cavani, 34, in it.

Rangnick replied that he was certain it could. The German was, of course, proved very wrong.

It is this kind of strange, blinkered hubris that we should not expect Mauricio Pochettino to bring with him to Old Trafford.

Heaven knows we have seen enough of that in recent times. Ruben Amorim and his back three. Erik ten Hag and… well maybe one day we will understand what all that was supposed to be about.

But no, this will not be Pochettino. This cannot be Pochettino.

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football. This is not Tottenham Hotspur 2016. It is not Kyle Walker, Toby Alderweireld, Son Heung-min and Harry Kane. It is not physical and youthful and energetic.

Mauricio Pochettino is waving goodbye to the US national team and hello to Man United this week. But he faces a daunting task at Old Trafford

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football

That is why Pochettino’s battle – at least for the remainder of this season – will be about hearts and minds as much as it is about anything revolutionary that he can bring to bear on the training fields of Carrington.

The good news for those hoping for quick improvement is that Pochettino – at least the one who took Spurs to a Champions League final in 2019 and to within a sniff of a Premier League title a few years earlier – is adept at the mental and emotional side of football. It is upon this that, initially at least, he may wish to rely.

Son told me about this when we sat down to look back on his career in England. He was prolific under Pochettino, a scorer of 75 goals in four-and-a-half seasons under the Argentine. But it was not always like that. Once – just like several current players at United – he was disaffected and unhappy.

‘Mauricio turned me round and it wasn’t about football,’ Son told me. ‘It was about me as a person and how he made he feel.

‘I needed help, basically. And he gave me it.

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words. It was unbelievable.

‘Sometimes he had been my coach and sometimes he had been like my family.’

Pochettino inherits a jigsaw puzzle with the wrong-shaped pieces at Old Trafford. It’s a squad put together for and by six different managers.

Pochettino will want to improve the fitness levels at United and his intense methods might feel like an ice bath to their players

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words,' says Son Heung-min of his manager at Tottenham. 'It was unbelievable... sometimes he was like my family’

On arrival this week, for example, he will renew acquaintances with Luke Shaw, one of his old Southampton players signed for Louis van Gaal at United back in 2014. Shaw – the club’s only real left back – is 31 now and recovering from injury.

The physical limitations of this United team were clear in the titanic but ultimately rather pitiful 4-4 draw with Aston Villa that proved to be Michael Carrick’s last game in charge just before the international break.

Invited back into a game they trailed 2-0, United’s front four briefly chased the life out of Villa when Unai Emery’s team were in possession. For 20 minutes, Villa could not get out of their own half.

But the likes of Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Amad Diallo simply could not maintain that level of exertion once the surge in adrenaline had spiked. By the time the game reached the hour mark, United were 4-2 down.

It is certain Pochettino will wish to improve some levels of fitness at United and his methods will perhaps feel like an ice bath to some of those United players who have approached the basic prerequisite of running like some kind of optional extra at times this season.

At Spurs, players were occasionally known to vomit during training. Pochettino told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

Six or seven years later at Chelsea, meanwhile, he punished striker Nicolas Jackson for picking up five largely needless yellow cards by ordering him to run laps of the training pitch. Jackson was only told why it was happening as he lay on the grass in a heap afterwards.

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa whose ‘Murderball’ sessions eventually arrived in England during his spell at Leeds United eight years ago. The stated aim is simple.

The likes of Bruno Fernandes (centre) have struggled to maintain the physicality Pochettino will demand across 90 minutes in games this season

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa

‘With Mauricio, there is no hiding,’ said former Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana on the Rest Is Football podcast.

‘Everything is high-intensity, pressing from the front, and repeating sprints again and again in training so that it becomes automatic on a Saturday.’

Trawl through Pochettino’s time as a frontline coach and the testimonies of unstinting, high-intensity work are strikingly similar. There has been no great change in the belief, even when he arrived in America to coach the US national team ahead of this summer’s World Cup.

'He brings that club intensity into the national team environment,’ says Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie. ‘You immediately feel the tempo he expects.’

For this to work well, a coach needs two things. A pre-season in which to embed that specific kind of fitness and a squad assembled to play that way.

At United, Pochettino has neither so we can expect it to be a slow burn. He is approaching the busiest period of the playing schedule – his team will play 12 games in the next six and a half weeks – and has immobile central defenders, full backs with limitations and a midfield unit that lacks legs when compared to the best in the Premier League and Europe.

Equally, Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new. Ten years ago, it was Klopp’s Liverpool. Now it’s Fabian Hurzeler’s Brighton and many, many others.

Every player has a brain and a mind, though, and it is here that Pochettino will in all likelihood seek to make the greatest gains ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and beyond.

Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new when he landed at Southampton in 2013

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight

There is not a United manager since the end of the Sir Alex Ferguson era who has not run into trouble with individual players at some point. Ten Hag with Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho and Raphael Varane. Amorim with Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo. Carrick with his captain, Fernandes.

This, as much as anything, is what has held United back this season. United do not have a squad fit to win the league but that it sits in the bottom three says everything for the way Carrick and his coaching staff failed at their side of the deal.

Pochettino’s friendship with Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment. Indeed, there are similarities to be found between the two. Pochettino, for example, is a small details man, a coach who understands that mood and motivation and cohesion can be just as important as tactics or indeed anything the opposition can bring on a Saturday afternoon.

Having reached out yesterday to a former Southampton player for input on his ex-manager’s methods, the former international gave an insight – albeit unwittingly – into the kind of loyalty Pochettino can inspire.

‘We need to let him integrate at United his own way,’ came the reply. ‘I don’t think he needs us talking about his secrets.’

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He was with Son. He was with Kane.

‘He said, “You need to do this and this and that’s why you’re not in the squad”,’ Kane once told Daily Mail Sport. ‘And it just hit me. This is what I’ve got to do.’

Equally, the 54-year-old trades in subtlety. At Tottenham, he would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in. He had staff video them at training and wondered why they always looked happier when they walked off at the end.

At Tottenham, Pochettino would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in

Pochettino’s friendship with Sir Alex Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment

As strange as it sounds, Pochettino chose the detergent in the washing room as he believed the smell of the first team kit was important. He dropped a player simply because he had noticed him eating stodgy food before sessions and another because he believed his choice of car to be inappropriate to his relative lowly standing in the game.

These are the kinds of things that look clever when you win and like new-age bunkum when you don’t. At Spurs, Pochettino’s results spoke for him but what is critical now is what version has walked through the door at Old Trafford.

It’s true that, to a large extent, we all view him as Pochettino 2016. In the decade that has followed, there have been underwhelming spells at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. His attempts at making the kind of emotional connections he thrives on in Paris, for example, soon ran into a brick wall with the words ‘Neymar’ and ‘Mbappe’ written on it.

To return to the Ferguson link again, Pochettino has not previously been shy of perceived similarities.

‘Ferguson used to tell his players that working hard is a talent,’ he wrote in his 2017 book Brave New World. ‘To me, if a player doesn’t work hard for the team, he won't play. Nothing happens by chance.’

What manager in football doesn’t value basic endeavour? Not one but, as mutual trust and shared belief starts to wane during a run of bad results, even the basics can get lost. With this in mind and with Pochettino’s energy and charisma in the building, it’s not unrealistic to expect a new manager bounce at Old Trafford.

His relationship with Fernandes will be crucial and the Portuguese should not expect the captaincy to be a given. At Tottenham, Pochettino gave it to his goalkeeper, Hugo Lloris.

Pochettino knows that coaches can’t speak to players the way they used to, or indeed may wish to. A greater degree of emotional intelligence is required.

Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez - both publicly critical of the set-up at United this season - can expect private words of advice from their new boss

Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford a wiser manager for working amid the background noise at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea

United’s players can therefore expect WhatsApp messages at 11pm at night – sometimes including attachments of training clips – quiet words of advice or observation when passing their manager in a corridor or even a short note, serious or otherwise, left in a dressing room locker. How the likes of Fernandes, Cunha, Rashford, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez respond to all this will be key.

So, too, will Pochettino’s ability or otherwise to make the best of the clunky chain of executive command that sits above him. At Tottenham, Pochettino and chairman Daniel Levy hit a sweet spot that wasn’t to last but for a time saw them so in tune they even took a horse-riding trip together. It was a synchronicity that electrified the whole football club.

Here in Manchester in 2026-27, it will feel different. At United, senior players criticise executives to the media while the fans wave green-and-gold scarves on matchday and sing unpleasant songs about not one but two different ownership groups. None of that will go away just because yet another manager is through the door.

Pochettino may feel he has some experience of such background noise from his time at PSG and indeed Chelsea. Equally, much of what happens over the course of the rest of this season and, if he is lucky, beyond will depend on his own reserves of energy, desire and self-regeneration. Does his own well remain deep enough?

The man who swept into Southampton with little-to-no English but bags of ideas and energy in January 2013 was an irresistible force of nature and he ran hot through the Premier League for a while. If he brings some of that to Old Trafford then he has a chance of making an impression at least.

But Pochettino’s take on Murderball, punishment laps and the infamous ‘Gacon’ 5km running drill he has been known to use may have to wait until the summer. United’s immediate issues, he will find, are more about a failing culture, centring less on playing style and more on emotional substance.

#1320. Como consider new striker after Kean injury problem

The unexpected Moise Kean setback could prompt a change of plan for Como in January, as they might need to invest in another centre-forward with Sergio Camello of Rayo Vallecano mentioned.

The Lariani already spent a lot of money convincing Fiorentina to sell Kean in the summer for €35m plus up to another €5m in add-ons.

However, after just four competitive appearances, he has been struggling with a recurring leg injury and might be out for a while longer.

Como released a statement confirming that Kean is undergoing further medical assessment following an issue in training, but the fear is he will be out until at least 2027.

That leaves Tasos Douvikas as the only available centre-forward, with Nico Paz potentially moving into a False 9 role on occasion.

It simply isn’t enough for a team in Serie A, the Champions League and Coppa Italia, so they are likely to push for another striker in the January transfer window.

According to Tuttomercatoweb, the primary target is Rayo Vallecano forward Sergio Camello.

A product of the Atletico Madrid youth academy, he was sold to Rayo in 2023 for €5m and his contract is due to expire at the end of the season, so he would be available relatively cheap.

Camello scored seven goals with nine assists in 11 LaLiga games so far this season.

#1319. 25 Greatest Goalkeepers in Football History (Ranked)

Behind every successful football team is a top-quality goalkeeper. Acting as the final barrier of defence, their crucial saves, last-minute heroics and composure in between the sticks can be the difference between success and failure.

An outfield player can make a mistake and get away with it; a goalkeeper can't. As they play with hopes and dreams on their backs, they have to perform at the highest level every week.

Elite goalkeepers are capable of winning points almost single-handedly and the very best are often held in the highest regard by the clubs they've starred for.

Liverpool struggled with Loris Karius in goal during 2018, as the German made two crucial mistakes to see the Reds lose the Champions League final to Real Madrid. They bought Alisson Becker in the summer of 2018, helping them win the Champions League a year later. It showcases how crucial they are.

To honour their efforts between the posts, here are the greatest goalkeepers of all time. Each player's selection and ranking has been carefully considered, using ranking factors which are outlined below.

Hugo Lloris was at the heart of Tottenham's modern-day 'golden era' from 2012 until 2024. He was their captain under manager Mauricio Pochettino, providing experience in the key matches. The Frenchman was a world-class goalkeeper season after season, with a string of penalty saves in the 2018/19 campaign helping Spurs secure Champions League football and reach the final.

However, he never won a trophy with the Lilywhites, unlike his time as France captain. Lloris became a world champion with Les Bleus in 2018, and he was unfortunate to miss out on a second World Cup winner's medal four years later. The former Tottenham captain was also a runner-up in the 2016 European Championships, but he was victorious in the 2020/21 UEFA Nations League. A stalwart between the posts for years, he went on to become his country's most-capped player, with manager Didier Deschamps hailing him as "exemplary" for his years of service.

Earning the nickname "the Iron Curtain," Rinat Dasayev made a name for himself with Spartak Moscow for remarkable saves. Spending most of his years at the Russian club in the 1980s, he was renowned for his one-handed stops and remarkable athleticism.

Dasayev was the Soviet Union's goalkeeper and captain during their impressive run to the finals of Euro 1988. He was a part of the side which beat England 3-1 to confirm the Three Lions' exit from the competition, but is arguably remembered most of all for being the 'keeper who was beaten in goal after Marco van Basten's stunning volley. Still, he'd been impressive enough at that tournament and throughout the year to be named the best goalkeeper in the world.

Michel Preud'homme came through the ranks at Standard Liege, spending nine years with the Belgian club before going on to represent Mechelen and then Portuguese titans Benfica. Although he was only at the Eagles for the final five years of his career, he earned the name 'Saint Michel' by supporters for his heroics between the posts.

On the international stage, Preud'homme was equally impressive. Having been a back-up 'keeper during the Red Devils' run to the final of Euro 1980, he took centre stage at the 1990 and 1994 World Cups, ensuring his country reached the round of 16. That tournament also saw him bestowed with the inaugural Yashin Award for the best goalkeeper at the tournament.

After coming through the ranks of Inter Milan and a series of loan moves to Salernitana, Savona and Sambenedettese, Walter Zenga was eventually given the opportunity to be the nerrazurri's number one. And he made the position his own for years before he departed the club in 1994.

Named the best goalkeeper in the world for three years, the Italian helped his side lift the Serie A in 1988/89, an impressive achievement considering how much of a powerhouse their rivals AC Milan were at that time. Also his country's first-choice shot-stopper, Zenga ensured Italy finished third at their home World Cup in 1990, repeating an achievement that the Azzurri managed at Euro 1988.

Inter Milan, Sampdoria, New England Revolution

Peter Shilton is one of the best English goalkeepers ever. He is most well-known for his contribution to Nottingham Forest's two European Cup triumphs in 1979 and 1980. Brian Clough heralded Shilton as being even better than World Cup-winning goalkeeper Gordon Banks, as he also helped the East Midlands club secure the First Division title in 1978.

Shilton made 125 appearances for his country, playing in some high-profile World Cup matches, including the quarter-final against Argentina, where Diego Maradona scored the infamous 'Hand of God' goal past him. Although he was unable to secure a major tournament for the Three Lions, he holds the record for the most caps for his country.

Leicester City, Stoke City, Nottingham Forest, Southampton, Derby, West Ham

Andoni Zubizarreta is a Spanish football legend, representing his country 126 times from 1985 to 1998. He played in seven major tournaments for his country, captaining his country to the 1994 and 1998 World Cups.

Zubizarretta also had an illustrious club career, playing for the likes of Barcelona, Valencia, and Athletic Bilbao. He won La Liga twice for the Basque side, including the league and cup double in the 1983/84 season, but his main success was in Catalonia. As a Barcelona player, Zubizarreta played an integral part in securing six La Liga titles, as well as the 1991/92 European Cup under the management of Johan Cruyff. The Spanish goalkeeper was ahead of his time in terms of his ability with the ball at his feet and ease under pressure.

Alaves, Athletic Bilbao, Barcelona, Valencia

In the annals of Spanish football, not many players have a legacy like Ricardo Zamora. Playing most of his football at Espanyol, he also featured for both Barcelona and Real Madrid during the 1920s and 30s, becoming one of La Roja's earliest football stars.

In 1930, Zamora was between the sticks as Spain became the first side outside the British Isles to beat England in a competitive match, playing with a broken sternum as his country ran out 4-3 victors. There is a common saying throughout Spain which underlines El Divino's incredible talent: "there are only two goalkeepers: Ricardo Zamora on Earth and St Peter in Heaven." Moreover, the goalkeeper with the lowest goals-to-game ratio in La Liga each season is now given the 'Zamora Trophy,' a testament to the goalkeeper's sporting legacy.

Espanyol, Barcelona, Real Madrid, OGC Nice

Dino Zoff was an ever-present member of the Juventus and Italy teams throughout the 1970s. His most notable achievement is undoubtedly his 1982 World Cup triumph for the Azzurri, where he captained the side to glory. After finishing runner-up in 1970, it was looking as if Zoff would go his whole career without a World Cup triumph, but 1982 saw the legendary goalkeeper win the trophy at the age of 40.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Dino Zoff is the oldest player to win the World Cup.

At club level, he was even more successful, winning six Serie A titles as well as two Coppa Italia titles and a UEFA Cup. Hailed as a "legend" by shot-stopper Gianluigi Buffon, the only thing that Zoff didn't tick off his resume was the European Cup. He was a runner-up in 1973 and a decade later, when Juventus lost to Hamburger SV.

Although most football supporters will name Pele or Garrincha first when asked about Brazil's World Cup-winning squads of 1958 and 1962, Gilmar was an equally important cog in the machinery. Arguably one of the best goalkeepers of the 20th century, he was the last line of defence for two of the Selecao's most famous triumphs on the international stage, conceding just four times in their 1958 success.

Along with his 93 caps for the national side, Gilmar was a key presence for both Corinthians and Santos during the 1950s and 60s. His calmness between the sticks saw him win multiple pieces of silverware, particularly with the latter, as he collected five Serie A titles, along with two Copa Libertadores.

Neville Southall began his career in English football at Bury in 1980, before joining Everton a year later. Southall spent 17 years at the Merseyside club, winning two league titles, two FA Cups, and the 1984/85 European Cup Winners' Cup. He remains the all-time record appearance holder for the Toffees and is still renowned as one of the best players in the club's history.

In the 1980s, Southall was well-recognised as the best goalkeeper in English football, with Jamie Carragher even naming him the best goalkeeper ever. In the 1984/85 title-winning campaign, Southall picked up the Football Writers' Association Footballer of the Year. He also made 92 appearances for Wales, making his debut on 27th May 1982.

Bury, Everton, Port Vale, Stoke City, Torquay, Bradford

#1318. Who is JJ Gabriel's Dad? Ex-Ireland International Who Played for Arsenal

JJ Gabriel is deemed to be one of the brightest young prospects in world football, and Manchester United faced an acrimonious public battle to keep him on their books at the tail-end of 2026, with some of Europe's elite clubs circling for the signature of a player who has drawn comparisons to both Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo.

That saga, which ran for months, finally came to an end in November 2026 as the talented teenager announced his departure from the club via the medium of a farewell video, which declared: "Manchester United will always be part of my story. Thank you for everything."

It is hardly a surprise to learn that Gabriel, who sports the name 'Gabriel Jr' on his shirt, is strongly supported and influenced by his father, who has been a vocal advocate throughout his career, including — to the chagrin of some — on social media. It is fair to say that the player's father occupies a significant role in his career.

Here, GIVEMESPORT brings you all you need to know about JJ Gabriel's father.

Joe O'Cearuill (sometimes written Ó Cearúill) is the father of JJ Gabriel. Born in north London on February 9, 1987, O'Cearuill was a professional footballer whose career spanned around 12 years and saw him play for clubs across England and Ireland.

His football CV includes clubs such as Arsenal, Watford, Brighton, Barnet and Forest Green Rovers, as well as full international honours with the Republic of Ireland.

Arsenal, Brighton, Forest Green Rovers, Republic of Ireland

O'Cearuill was a defender during his career, featuring in the centre-back and right-back positions - a stark contrast to his son, who is very much an attacker inspired by the likes of Messi and Ronaldo, two of the greatest football players of all time.

Though born in England, O'Cearuill has links to Trinidad and Tobago through his father and Ireland through his mother, whose connection is to the south-western county of Cork. These connections benefit his son, who is eligible for a number of countries as a result.

JJ Gabriel's real full name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill. According to reports, his name was changed in a bid to make it more marketable.

All you need to know about the wonderkid tipped to be the next big thing in football

O'Cearuill began his football journey in 2004 as a youth player for Leyton Orient before moving on to Watford and eventually earning a professional contract with Arsenal in 2006.

He played mostly for the Gunners' reserve teams, but trained with the first team and featured on the bench in a number of games. While on the books at Arsenal, he spent a brief spell on loan at Brighton, who were then playing in League One, and featured in a testimonial game for Dennis Bergkamp.

During his time as an Arsenal player, O'Cearuill earned call-ups to the Ireland Under-21 and senior squads. He made two senior appearances for the Boys in Green under Steve Staunton, playing in friendly games against Ecuador and Bolivia in the United States. The image above shows him in action against Aaron Lennon and the England U-21s.

Came off the bench for Stephen O'Halloran on the 73rd minute and received a yellow card.

Started and played full 90 minutes alongside Alan Bennett at centre-back.

As well as playing for clubs across England, O'Cearuill had a short spell in Ireland with St Patrick's Athletic in 2008, which saw him play for the club in the UEFA Cup against the likes of Hertha Berlin.

O'Cearuill is generally perceived as a 'journeyman' footballer, due to the fact that he played for a large number of teams and spent relatively brief periods at each. He concluded his playing days in 2016 at Haringey Borough.

The England wonderkid was desperate for a move away after United rejected some of his demands.

#1315. Football Manager 27 Wonderkids: Best Young Players to Buy in FM27

You've loaded up a new game on Football Manager 27 and you have a vision: build the best young team in the world and dominate for years. Unless you have one of the best academies in football, the only way you can do this is by recruiting as many wonderkids as possible.

A wonderkid is a young talent who possesses high potential and, with the right attitude, support and training, will evolve into a world-class player. You're looking for the next Cristiano Ronaldo or Lionel Messi, two of the greatest football players of all time. You're scouting for youth prospects who have what it takes to become the next big thing in football, whether that's in the mould of a swashbuckling centre-back such as Paolo Maldini, a formidable goalkeeper like Manuel Neuer or an all-action midfield dynamo akin to the Ballon d'Or-winning Rodri.

Here, GIVEMESPORT brings you the best wonderkid goalkeepers, defenders, midfielders and strikers, aged 20 and under, based on potential ability.

(Key: CA = Current Ability, PA = Potential Ability)

German duo Dennis Seimen and Florian Hellstern are the two best young goalkeepers in Football Manager 27, closely followed by Japanese prospect Rui Araki. Of that trio, Araki is the most affordable, and could mature into one of the best goalkeepers in the world if nurtured well by the right manager.

Dutch shotstopper Quenten Attigah has a very high ceiling, but may take some time to reach his potential given that he is only 17, but if you want to land a talented young netminder who can do a job straight away, you should consider scouting Pierce Charles.

Romario Cunha would be a decent signing for a team looking to climb divisions and would be affordable too, while Brazilian youngster Joao Pedro (not that one) is also a bargan at under £1 million.

To get you started on your journey to world domination in EA Sports FC 27, here are the best young players to buy in the game

It will come as little surprise to learn that Pau Cubarsi is top of the pile when it comes to wonderkid defenders in FM27 and he is virtually not for sale with Barcelona placing a mammoth valuation on his head. So it will take a lot of money and a lot of convincing to land his services in the game.

Brighton's centre-back Luka Vuskovic, one of the nominees for the 2026 Golden Boy award, is a more achievable target, but he will still command a hefty fee. If you're limited when it comes to budget, have a look at Inter Milan's Leondaro Bovio or Coventry City's Stephen Mfuni. If you're in the market for a left-back, do what you can to sign Saba Kharebashvili, who is primed to be one of the best left-backs in the world, according to FM's stats gurus.

Who will be taking Pau Cubarsi's crown in 2027?

Lamine Yamal is the player with the highest potential in the game, and the best midfielder, but, much like his compatriot and team-mate Cubarsi, is practically unattainable, unless you're a manager who is capable of unsettling big-name stars and convincing them to join your crusade. Yamal is joined by the likes of Estevao and Yan Diomande, as well as Rio Ngumoha and Ayyoub Bouaddi, all among the best young players in world football, at the top of the list.

A little bit further down in terms of potential ability is Luca Williams-Barnett, who is more suited to an attacking role, while Mahdi Nicoli-Jazuli could morph into one of the best Number 10s in the game. Reggie Walsh, meanwhile, will be up there with Bouaddi as one of the best defensive midfielders around, should he reach his potential.

USMNT wonderkid Cavan Sullivan is just outside this list, but the playmaker is certainly worth scouting, though he will be difficult to lure given his profile.

Aston Villa's imposing young striker Brian Madjo looks well placed to grow into the best out-and-out strikers in the game alongside Endrick, who has been a fixture of these lists for the past few years. It is worth looking to France and Italy for upcoming wonderkid strikers, with 16-year-old Montpellier prospect Lacine Megnan appearing particularly impressive. Roma have Antonio Arena in their ranks, while AC Milan's Francesco Camarda boasts similar potential.

If you are managing a club that is somewhat strapped for cash, here is a selection of the top wonderkids valued at £10 million or less.

The aforementioned Megnan features, but the best of the bunch looks to be Joshua Abe, Liverpool's exciting young winger. The United States is represented by Christopher Cupps and Gabriel Wesseh, both of whom would represent decent business.

Of course, in some cases, a loan move might be the only option, but there is satisfaction to be had in playing a part in a player's development. Indeed, if a young starlet has a positive experience at your club, who is to say they won't be inclined to stick around, or return at a later date?

If your budget is so tight that you need to keep things under the multimillion mark in the transfer market, here are a few players worth scouting.

Some of football's most exciting prospects can be found on FM 26.

#1313. Emotional Mauricio Pochettino gets perfect sendoff in his US farewell... before boarding jet for new life as Manchester United manager

By ALEX RASKIN, US SPORTS NEWS EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER

Published: 21:06 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 00:56 EST, 18 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino received a near-perfect sendoff as US men's national team head coach on Tuesday in Cincinnati, where Manchester United's next manager watched his now-former players beat Haiti before bidding an emotional farewell to his adopted country.

Christian Pulisic, Pochettino's brightest pupil over the last two seasons, rose to the occasion by scoring on a gravity-defying bicycle kick in the 25th minute and 18-year-old prospect Julian Hall followed in the 43rd with a goal of his own.

But for all of the excitement on the field – where Pochettino helped rebuild the American attack with a high-intensity style – all eyes were on the manager as he embraced his team one last time.

With the 2-0 win (8-0 aggregate), the USMNT now advances to the CONCACAF Nations League semifinals, but that's no longer Pochettino's concern. Instead, former American fullback and current under-23 manager Steve Cherundolo is expected to take over on an interim basis, while Pochettino turns his attention to an 18th-place United squad that has just one win in the English Premier League through 10 matches this season.

'When you finish the game, you start in your mind to think about different things,' Pochettino said after the win. 'Of course, it's tough because it's emotional. Because I really love these guys, and I love the players. I love the staff. I love the fans and everything.'

Following the win, Pochettino was scheduled to fly from northern Kentucky to Manchester aboard a private plane chartered by his new club. The quick escape offered the chance to avoid major airlines following Friday's chaotic nationwide shutdown, and perhaps a few hours' sleep for a 54-year-old starting his new job on Wednesday at Carrington Training Centre.

Pochettino spent two years with the USMNT, helping to rebuild an attack around Pulisic

Pochettino hugs a staff member prior to the CONCACAF Nations League Quarterfinal match

Pochettino paces along a near-empty sideline after much of his staff left for Manchester

And Pochettino didn't plan on traveling alone.

Outgoing USMNT first-team coach Miguel D'Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott were expected to join Pochettino aboard the flight to Manchester, where assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez as well as Pochettino's son and fitness coach Sebastiano have already begun preparing for Sunday's matchup with Liverpool at Anfield.

The quick turnaround means Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty. Furthermore, he is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference around lunchtime on Friday.

The Argentine national is replacing Michael Carrick at Old Trafford on a two-and-a-half year contract after United agreed to pay more than £10million ($13m) to buy him and his backroom staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation.

Before boarding his flight, Pochettino not only waved to his adoring fans, but took a photo with staff and players on the pitch in Cincinnati.

'It's impossible not to cry, but that is because we care about the people and the people care about us,' he told reporters. 'When that happens, it's normal to show your emotions, no? Because we are human. We are no robots.'

Mauricio Pochettino saying his final goodbyes to the USA fans as he's now gonna fly to Manchester immediately ❤️ pic.twitter.com/sCe8LCjpK5

Pulisic, perhaps Pochettino's brightest pupil, scored on a bicycle kick in the 25th minute

Pulisic celebrates his goal on Tuesday night in Cincinnati during the win over Haiti

Pochettino was expected to board a flight from northern Kentucky to Manchester after the win

Pochettino had been on something of a farewell tour in the US, where he embraced the local sports scene over his brief tenure. In between overseeing his final games with the USMNT, Pochettino was spotted at the Cincinnati Bengals' win over the visiting Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday.

The manager, sporting his blue USSF coat, was captured standing on the sidelines with members of his staff ahead before kickoff, where he mingled with Bengals special teamers such as kicker Evan McPherson, long snapper William Wagner and punter Ryan Rehkow.

A night earlier, Pochettino guided the US to a 6-0 win over Haiti in Miami to give his team a safe cushion for his farewell on Tuesday in Cincinnati.

Pochettino broke down in tears as he announced his decision last week, while admitting he couldn't turn down the 'dream' job with Manchester United.

Mauricio Pochettino walks on the field after the CONCACAF Nations League Quarterfinal

American fans give Pochettino a standing ovation in Cincinnati after his farewell match

Flanked by US Soccer Federation bosses at the team's headquarters in Georgia, an emotional Pochettino wiped away tears as he thanked the players and staff.

'I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,' he said. 'It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

'I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

'Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

'In some part it's a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'

United will pay the US Soccer Federation more than $13.2 million (£10m) in compensation for Pochettino and his backroom staff.

'I never said I wanted to go back in the Premier League,' Pochettino, a former Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton boss, told reporters last week. 'All of this was so quick because we arrived here last Friday and on Sunday afternoon this type of situation started to appear.'

Pochettino turns his attention to an 18th-place United squad that has just one EPL win

Mauricio Pochettino insisted it was the 'most difficult decision' to leave the USMNT

Pochettino put together a 23-12-2 record with the US, while 78 players earned caps for the US over his tenure. Remarkably, nine teenagers made their USMNT debuts for Pochettino, including Hall, who scored on Tuesday.

But the Americans failed to crack into the sport's upper echelon during Pochettino's brief tenure in the US. In his lone World Cup appearance with the team last summer, Pochettino guided the USMNT to the Round of 16, where the Americans fell to Belgium, 4-1.

That result was an improvement on 2018, when the US failed to qualify, but not on 2022, when then-coach Gregg Berhalter's similarly team fell short of the quarters with a 3-1 loss to the Netherlands.

Despite this, Pochettino's American players have remained largely supportive of his tenure, including Berhalter's son Sebastian, who said the outgoing coach helped him 'develop as a player and as a person.'

Prior to Tuesday's win, Pochettino thanked American fans for the support he received over his two years with the national team.

'Thank you so much from the bottom of my heart for all the fans, for all the people that was supporting us in the last two years,' Pochettino said in a video posted on social media. 'Special, great memories of the World Cup and everything that we lived together. Always in my heart, always one of you. All the best and I wish everything good for the future.'

Potential candidates to replace Pochettino in the US include former Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola, ex-England manager Gareth Southgate and some lesser-known candidates like Cherundolo, who now guides the United States U-23 team.

'For us to win, we need to be great at a lot of things, and we need someone who cares about youth development, cares about our youth national team programs, our relationships with our clubs and the success of the federation more broadly,' US Soccer CEO JT Batson told TNT Sports on Tuesday. 'We know that is a key part of our success, and it's also a key part of how we've been able to attract great people because they get to do big things.'

#1310. You're Not Nineteenth Forever! Sacked Man United manager Michael Carrick looks relieved to be out of the relegation fight as he watches The Courteeners at gig in London

Published: 04:29 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 05:44 EST, 18 November 2026

Former Man United boss Michael Carrick was seen enjoying some time out of the spotlight as he watched The Courteeners at a gig in London over the weekend.

Carrick, 45, was relieved of his duties as United boss on Thursday following a dismal start to the season that has seen his former side pick up just eight points and one victory in ten matches.

That came despite his incredible impact in the second half of last season when he replaced Ruben Amorim and led the Red Devils to third place in the Premier League.

And on Saturday night, a few days after his tenure ended, Carrick attended a tour date of The Courteeners.

According to the band's schedule, they were performing at Alexandra Palace in London.

One fan shared a photo on X from the gig, with the caption 'One hell of a day out'.

Michael Carrick was spotted watching The Courteneers at a gig in London over the weekend (Source X/adamkearey)

In the shot, Carrick looked relaxed and was smiling as he tried to make the most of a rare Saturday off.

The Courteeners were formed in Manchester and their frontman Liam Fray is known to be a lifelong United fan.

He regularly shared praise for Carrick during his time in the Old Trafford dugout, including backing him to get the best out of Marcus Rashford on his return to the club after his loan spell at Barcelona.

Some of The Courteeners' most famous songs include Are You In Love With A Notion? and Not Nineteen Forever, ironically the position United were in under Carrick until their 96th-minute equaliser against Aston Villa before the international break took them up to 18th place.

Following his sacking on Thursday after ten months in charge, Carrick issued a heartfelt statement reflecting on his tenure.

Posting on social media, he said: ‘I’ve had the immense privilege of leading Manchester United, the football club that I love.

‘There are very few who get to live that and feel it, and for that I’m incredibly grateful. I want to say a big thank-you to the supporters. I must say, you are a special, rare breed.

‘I know we’ve not had the results lately, but you’ve shown me nothing but love and support in times when the easiest thing, and what most end up doing, would be to turn the other way.

‘That’s what makes you who you are. That’s why I fell in love with this club all those years ago.’

Carrick was relieved of his duties at Man United on Thursday after a dismal start to the season

The axe ultimately fell on Carrick on Thursday, yet the writing was on the wall for several days beforehand as speculation spread and United's hierarchy worked towards an agreement with Mauricio Pochettino.

Many former United stars were hugely critical of their former club, with Gary Neville calling their treatment of Carrick 'disgusting', while Peter Schmeichel labelled it 'very disrespectful'.

Rio Ferdinand also compared United's 142-word statement announcing his sacking to 'like ChatGPT' after there was no comment added by club chiefs.

United are back in action on Sunday when they travel to Anfield to take on Liverpool in what will be Pochettino's first game in charge.

#1309. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Is there anything Harry Kane can't do? 🧐 His goal kick very nearly led to a Bayern Munich goal 😲 https://t.co/fqbsN7KOjw

And then Bayern did score. The ball was played inside to Kane, in centre field and afforded too much space. He delivered a perfectly weighted through ball for Alphonse Davies to run on to. The pace was perfect, allowing the Canadian not to break stride and stroke it past Raya. Kane did not fire the ball in, he did not make Davies work to reach it and he did not give Jurrien Timber any chance of cutting it out. It was perfect. Few players could do that. “Harry Kane puts the ball in a space from 30 metres that doesn’t exist,” Arteta said. True.

It was Saka’s replacement who gave Arsenal the lead, Eberechi Eze profiting from Martin Odegaard’s perceptive, lofted pass and taking advantage of Bayern’s ragged defending and some suspect goalkeeping from 40-year-old Neuer to score from an angle. Harry Kane, what a penalty 🥶 He scores in his TENTH consecutive Champions League game to give Bayern the lead 😳 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/4k4jPCQEWF

They were rewarded as Rice started the move, playing the ball in quickly to Noni Madueke with substitute Viktor Gyokeres laying it back into the midfielder’s path. It had similarities [with last year’s league phase game]. I think we managed to create more chances but I think that Arsenal – and it’s something that has been mentioned by them before the game – they’ve worked a lot on retaining the ball and making it difficult to get the ball back. We did feel that.

It was a game in chunks. They had moments, we had moments. In our moments, I think we exploited the spaces in behind a little bit better maybe but we played against a top team and the result is a result between two big teams.

Last year they reaped the benefits of a top-two finish: home ties all the way to the final and a guarantee of avoiding the other club in the top two.

They have a chance to pick off Real Madrid at the Emirates, and will anticipate Aston Villa (who still have to play Barcelona and PSG) and Real Betis dropping points.

Given PSG have already dispatched Manchester City and Barcelona, it is hard to envisage them dropping a point, though they do have the odd off night.

Arsenal’s chances of grabbing second could come down to winning their remaining games and Liverpool slipping up. But with five games to go, these permutations are probably premature.

Wow, what a game. That is one of the highest levels that we have played. The level of opposition, what the game required, and our level as well. Two teams who wanted to press each other and wanted to attack and wanted to play. It was a fascinating game.

I think we started the game incredibly well, we were so dominant, we did everything to deserve the first goal. We didn’t score the goal and lost Bukayo and had to adapt to it.

We gave a terrible chance away after our corner which could have cost us, then we scored the goal. In the second half, the game was even,  they started probably a little bit better before they scored and they you have to react and we certainly did.

The spirit of the team, the quality we have showed on the second goal as well.

They are a bit concerned. A player having to come off with a sharp pain is never good news but we have to wait and see.

For me he’s the clear winner, his numbers speak for themselves. He’s obviously up against some other world class players. When you play with him you see how good it is, and when you play against him you see how much of a pain he is! As a striker to play that pass for the goal... he’s ridiculous. Lucky I can play with him, not so lucky when I have to play against him.

I thought it was a good performance. Probably the draw was a fair result overall. We probably just didn’t get quite enough right tonight to get the win.

Nice to get the assist to get back into the game and then I thought we had some good moments but not enough over the 90 minutes.

When you play against teams like Bayern who are man to man all over the pitch you have to apply certain principles, and I just kept running and managed to get away from my man. When they are following you all over, I just kept running and I was in on the goal.

He’s been making such a good impact from the bench [Gyokeres]. He’s made some great runs tonight and set me up for the goal. When you play against man to man, who follow you everywhere over the whole pitch, it’s such a tough game. You have to apply certain principles and concepts, and you’re constantly thinking about where the space is. For the goal, Noni one-touch set, Viktor’s one-touch set, those little movements put you through on goal.

In periods of the game, it felt like Arsenal were trying to play in the manner of Bayern or PSG by leaving themselves so light at the back with acres of green grass to cover.

Would they play like that in a quarter-final? Probably not, and they were emboldened by Bayern missing some key players. But it helped them create danger and have some strong spells, even if there were some scary moments going the other way.

Somewhere between that display and Arsenal’s rearguard in the Champions League final is probably the sweet spot.

A high-quality game between two of the most plausible winners of this season’s Champions League finishes level.

It was a helter-skelter contest at times. For all the talk of Arteta being a conservative coach, Arsenal committed numbers forward in their press and when they attacked, and that left them vulnerable to Bayern’s fast transitions and Kane’s passes from deep.

Perhaps it is a missed opportunity to beat Bayern in the Allianz, given the German side started without Olise, Kimmich, Musiala and Diaz, but a point from the hardest fixture of the league phase is more than acceptable.

The fly in the ointment is the injury suffered by Saka in the first half, but Eze and Madueke performed well in his absence.

Just one minute to play and Bayern have the ball in Arsenal’s half, but Calafiori gets his foot in. Madueke does well to keep it and Lewis-Skelly finds Eze.

Timber with dig from outside the box after a poor defensive header from Bayern, and Neuer tips it over. Rice to take the corner, and Arsenal’s set-pieces have caused problems throughout. This might just be Arsenal’s chance to win it.

Swung to the back post, but Tah did enough.

Bayern had an injury worry of their own now: Luis Diaz, not judged fit to start, has pulled up and will have to come off. Bayern were in a promising position in the Arsenal half.

Harry Kane looking for another of those arced passes forward, but Eze read it and retrieved. Arsenal finishing the stronger when it comes to possession and territory. Perhaps that Premier League intensity bearing fruit as the game progresses.

A couple of fouls given away by both teams, it has been a bitty few minutes. But Arsenal do well to find Lewis-Skelly free in the middle of the pitch, and he finds Rice who drives the away team forward.

Neither team appears inclined to settle for the draw, but Arsenal have the wind in their sails. Mikel Merino is on for Martin Odegaard, who has probably been Arsenal’s best player on the night.

Arsenal back level again, and it is an emphatic finish across Neuer from Rice, after a deft touch from Gyokeres around the corner at the edge of the box. Bright football around the box from Arsenal. Still 10 minutes or so to play.

Arsenal have been scoring gorgeous team goals all season. They have done so in all three of their Champions League games this season. They were labelled as “boring” after the Forest victory but that game was the exception, rather than the rule, on the evidence of this campaign.

Arsenal deep in Bayern territory after Rice’s cross towards Eze glanced off the head of a defender. Bayern are keeping a good defensive shape though, Arsenal finding it difficult to penetrate. Arteta is preparing another pair of changes.

Luis Diaz with a snap shot that brings a sharp save from David Raya. On the balance of chances and threat created, Bayern have earned their lead. But still plenty of football to play. This is a proper heavyweight clash but, sadly for the neutrals watching, Bayern are missing some big players. Michael Olise is suspended, Jamal Musiala is injured and Joshua Kimmich is unavailable following the death of his father.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Ice cold from Martinelli 🥶 https://t.co/uQEHb4x7eH

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

Milan star Christian Pulisic left his mark in Mauricio Pochettino’s final game as USMNT coach by scoring a stunning bicycle-kick goal against Haiti.

Eighteen years ago, Bournemouth were minutes away from being liquidated and playing in the fourth tier. On Thursday night, Bournemouth not only welcomed AC Milan in Europe; they did so as favourites, and then pummelled them.

When Amine Adli curled in an 84-minute free-kick with his left foot at the Vitality Stadium, it put the seal on the most extraordinary evening in Bournemouth’s history. On a brutally windy and wet night, Bournemouth trounced AC Milan 3-0.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1304. Harry Kane up for ANOTHER prize alongside three England team-mates - as Globe Soccer Awards voting opens ahead of glitzy Dubai ceremony

Published: 04:11 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 09:13 EST, 18 November 2026

Harry Kane is one of the main contenders for the prestigious Best Men's Player prize at the Globe Soccer Awards - and you can vote for the winner.

The Ballon d'Or king is joined by England team-mates Jude Bellingham, Declan Rice, and Bukayo Saka in the category.

Meanwhile, Lionesses star Alessia Russo is the sole English representative in contention for the Best Women's Player honour.

Voting is now open across 12 categories, with the awards to be handed out at a glitzy ceremony in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on December 28.

The Globe Soccer Awards began in 2010 and have since became popular among fans worldwide, with more than 100 million votes cast in some years.

Last year's winner Ousmane Dembele is also in the running for Best Men's Player, with Lionel Messi, Lamine Yamal, and Kylian Mbappe joining him in the 26-strong shortlist.

Harry Kane, pictured with the Ballon d'Or, is among the nominees for Best Men's PLayer at the Globe Soccer Awards

Voting is now open across 12 award categories ahead of a ceremony in Dubai in December

Erling Haaland won the Best Men's Player prize for 2023 and is in contention again

Premier League stars Erling Haaland, Bruno Fernandes, William Saliba, and Dominik Szboszlai are also hoping to get their hands on the prize.

Mikel Arteta and Unai Emery are in the running for Best Coach, while Myles Lewis-Skelly and Nico O'Reilly are competing for the Emerging Player gong.

There are 14 categories, with a 'Career and Special Awards' section yet to see its talent announced.

Arsenal are hopefuls in the Best Club category for both men and women, with Aston Villa joining them in the former and Manchester City in the latter.

There will also be prizes for the best forward, midfielder, defender, and goalkeeper, and Fans' Historic Club, Best Sporting Director, and Best Agent.

Ronaldo, a serial winner at the ceremony, is defending his Best Middle East Player crown after winning his first Saudi Pro League title with Al-Nassr. Ivan Toney is among his rivals for that.

Fans are able to cast their votes until November 30, after which a jury including the likes of Antonio Conte and Luis Figo will also have their say.

It is an event of truly global interest, with supporters from more than 225 countries having cast votes in previous editions.

'We are incredibly proud to return for our third consecutive year as title partner of the GLOBE SOCCER Awards,' said Adil Taqi, CEO of title sponsor BEYOND Developments.

'Our continued partnership reflects BEYOND Developments’ commitment to connecting with an international audience through shared passions and experiences.

'Football brings people together across cultures and borders, resonating with our belief in pushing boundaries and aiming higher, a mindset shared by the players, coaches and clubs who will be honoured this December. We are proud to stand alongside an event that unites the global football family.'

Fans are able to vote via the Globe Soccer App.

#1303. Ex-Napoli striker takes aim at Allegri over Hojlund with cryptic social media post

Former Napoli striker Roberto Sosa took a cryptic dig at Massimiliano Allegri, asking why Rasmus Hojlund keeps scoring for Denmark while struggling to match those numbers for Napoli.

Hojlund has just started his second season at Napoli, but has only managed three goals in 14 appearances across all competitions under new coach Allegri.

His numbers with the Danish national team are very different, as the former Manchester United striker has netted six goals in his last six international appearances.

Sosa, a former Napoli striker, seems convinced that Hojlund’s poor form is tied to Allegri’s tactics.

“After dinner, after a nice digestif, don’t the coach’s friends ever ask themselves why the striker always scores for his national team but doesn’t score nearly as many goals (at least so far) for his club? Enjoy your meal,” Sosa wrote on X.

Sosa’s posts drew mixed reactions from Napoli fans, with some urging him to be less critical of the team and others backing his views.

Therefore, the former Argentine striker shared another post, this time a video from the seaside.

“After you’ve watched this video, you are free to write to me: ‘Pampa, I’m going to block you.’ And I’ll react with a heart,” he said.

“I watch every Napoli game, every Serie A, Premier League and European competition. If a team plays badly, I can’t say otherwise; I have to examine ball possession, counter-pressing, how they track back, and how they try to win those games. Then, I might note injuries, whether certain teams didn’t buy any players. But to me, we shouldn’t start backward, as some do, creating excuses or alibis. Well, those are the famous like-chasers. I wish you a good day, a good lunch and a good dinner!”

#1302. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

🗣️ Commitment. Resilience. Teamwork. Michael's powerful message in full 👇 https://t.co/vWwJt1fW47

This was partly Carrick reasserting his own authority after a couple of weeks in which two senior players – defender Lisandro Martínez and captain Bruno Fernandes – decided to go public with their grievances and the team delivered a performance in the 4-1 hammering by Como that was up there with the very worst.

But a stony-faced Carrick was also sending a message to his squad to quit their public sniping and start pulling together for a wider cause. Moreover, to put the club and the team before yourself and your individual needs and complaints.

It was interesting that he used the word “entitlement”. His predecessor, Ruben Amorim, had uttered that same word to attack what he felt was an “entitlement culture” at the club and Carrick has evidently come to a similar conclusion.

"I think it's the feeling of entitlement that we have in our club" Ruben Amorim says some of the players at Manchester United may need a bit of a reality check 🎙️ https://t.co/PiJWML3TeH

In truth, so many of the post-Ferguson managers have spoken in similar ways – certainly Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Jose Mourinho and Ralf Rangnick.

Listening to Carrick repeatedly talking about the need for humility, hard work, pride, sacrifice and resilience was a reminder of how the values that were once taken for granted at this football club have steadily been eroded.

Wayne Rooney said this week that United’s players were “selfish” and “babies”. Many top players over the years have been selfish but it helped drive them and, in turn, their team to great heights, but the same cannot be said about the current bunch.

Carrick spoke about trying to rediscover something that is “lost” at the moment. Whether they can is a big if. Opponents aside, the only winners at the moment from United’s latest crisis are Amazon.

Carrick had clearly thought hard about how he was going to tackle that today and what message he wanted to get across. The foundations of this football club and values have been etched down for many years.

No definitive answer from Carrick, who says he wants to do what is best for the football club.

There ends the broadcast section of the press conference after about 15 minutes.

Definitely a change in communication strategy from Carrick, speaking from the heart rather than waiting for questions.

My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club, represents the supporters and they can be proud of it with the identity that we show.

We have gone away from that just recently in certain games, which I’m fully aware of and definitely doing something about.

I think it’s important we all recognise that. I certainly recognise it. Our supporters of are the utmost importance to me and this football club.

For them to feel like they felt for five months at the start of the year and have that about us, that connection and that real vigour, intensity and enjoyment and passion is something we need to get back to.

Carrick says the dressing room is “not divided” but says it’s pretty clear the squad and everyone have to pull together and stop speaking out like has happened in public in response to questions about Martinez and Fernandes’ outbursts.

Principles are so important. We can win games, lose games, hopefully not but it can happen.

It’s how you do it and what it feels like is important for me. That the spirit and togetherness is there. It will be there. I’m working on solutions to move us forward.
